title: Digital consumer exposure can become a recovery and recourse problem without a common harm rate
source_unit: Bounded cross-source comparison of FTC administrative reports, Federal Reserve and SHED household surveys, and CFPB published complaint-response records; sources are not pooled

denominator.unit: 2024 total Sentinel reports; fraud and loss measures use their reported sub-universes

median_fraud_loss_2024.unit: US dollars among reports with loss

observations.method: FTC Consumer Sentinel administrative-report comparison across annual reports; reports are consumer or agency submissions, not a probability sample of incidents.
observations.uncertainty: Reported volume and loss are affected by reporting, classification, duplicate screening, and awareness. They do not estimate all fraud, platform causation, account-denominated incidence, or successful recovery.
observations.subgroup: Reports with usable age information show different reporting-loss shares and median losses by age.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stable or changing report volume can reflect reporting behavior and system visibility rather than underlying victimization; higher reported loss can reflect improved reporting of high-dollar cases.

investment_scam_reported_losses.unit: US dollars reported lost, more than

imposter_reported_losses.unit: US dollars reported lost, more than

observations.method: FTC 2025 Consumer Sentinel annual report frame; category totals are reported administrative losses.
observations.uncertainty: Reported losses are not population incidence, verified account losses, or proof that digital platforms caused the contact. Category totals and approximate counts use different reporting frames.
observations.counterinterpretation: A larger reported loss total may reflect more reporting, more high-value scams, or improved classification rather than a uniform increase in individual exposure.

observations.period: 2024; Federal Reserve SHED household fraud and recovery estimates

denominator.unit: weighted adult-population estimate; publication percentages use item-specific adult or fraud-experiencer universes

estimated_net_consumer_loss.unit: US dollars estimated borne directly by consumers

non_credit_card_fraud_some_money_not_rec.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

spent_ten_or_more_hours_recovering_or_de.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud, approximate

observations.method: Federal Reserve Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking descriptive estimates of self-reported fraud exposure, loss, recovery, and time cost.
observations.uncertainty: The estimates depend on self-report, recall, weighting, and question universes. They do not identify the originating platform, firm responsibility, verified remedy, or later trust and switching.
observations.subgroup: Adults, fraud experiencers, and age groups; credit-card and non-credit-card fraud are distinct surfaces.
observations.counterinterpretation: Recovery effort can be costly while a household remains financially stable; unrecovered money does not alone identify institutional blame or durable hardship.

denominator.unit: SHED public-use adult respondent rows; conditional outcomes use non-credit-card fraud reporters

other_fraud_unrecovered_income_10000_249.unit: percent of other-fraud reporters in income group

other_fraud_unrecovered_income_100000_14.unit: percent of other-fraud reporters in income group

account_fraud_p2p_unrecovered.unit: percent of account-involved other-fraud cases marked P2P with some or all money unrecovered

observations.method: Reproducible SHED public-use subgroup analysis with weighted conditional shares; payment-route and income cells retain distinct universes.
observations.uncertainty: These are descriptive conditional estimates, not causal income or payment-route effects. Small cells, self-report, fraud classification, and missingness limit interpretation.
observations.subgroup: Income bands and peer-to-peer versus non-peer-to-peer account-fraud routes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Income gradients may reflect differences in exposure, reporting, loss size, account use, recovery resources, or case composition rather than unequal institutional treatment.

denominator.unit: 2025 published complaint records; each annual measure uses its own published-record denominator

observations.method: CFPB published complaint records grouped by calendar year received and coded response fields; the dataset is a visible institutional endpoint, not a representative consumer panel.
observations.uncertainty: Publication rules, product mix, routing, screening, duplicates, missing fields, and firm-response coding change over time. Explanation or relief labels are not verified consumer outcomes.
observations.subgroup: All published complaints in the annual comparison; product-conditioned records in the underlying source remain separate.
observations.counterinterpretation: A low monetary-relief label can coexist with non-monetary resolution or a complaint that sought explanation rather than compensation; a published complaint need not represent unresolved harm.

related_sources.claim: CFPB publishes complaint records and response fields used as an institutional-visibility endpoint.
FTC AI-companion inquiry supplies a separate product-scrutiny route for data, monetization, safety, age limits, and disclosures.

boundary: This is a deliberately non-pooled digital-consumer and recourse triangulation. It connects reported exposure, household loss and recovery, subgroup burden, and complaint-system visibility as separate stages, but does not establish platform causation, a common fraud rate, verified remedy, consumer welfare, firm liability, trust change, switching, or exit. The end-to-end test still requires a dated customer or household episode linked to originating contact, loss, recovery effort, complaint, remedy, repeat effort, and later behavior.
